newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -- NY/NJ Port Authority chief Marlin.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -- NY/NJ Port Authority chief Marlin.

text.p: "Projects are off the drawing board and shovels are in the ground," outgoing New York and New Jersey Port Authority executive director George Marlin said, reflecting on the end of his term at the agency.

Marlin, whose almost two-year tenure in office has been marked with controversy and accomplishment, gave notice to New Jersey Gov Christine Whitman and New York State Gov George Pataki on Friday that he will not seek reappointment to a third one-year term when his term expires April 3.
In letters to Whitman and Pataki, Marlin said he has decided to return to the private sector.

"I laid the foundation here for reorganizing the Port Authority," Marlin said in a telephone interview with Reuters. "It is a solid foundation and I pass the baton on to the next person who will carry out the agenda of the two governors."
He cited among his accomplishments eliminating 1,300 positions, or 15 percent, of the agency's staff, and cutting its operating budget for the first time since 1943.
Marlin also noted that he was able to avoid toll and fare increases, and privatized the Vista Hotel in Manhattan and industrial parks in Yonkers and Elizabeth.

A conservative party candidate for New York City mayor in 1993, Marlin became a controversial appointee to the authority after Gov Whitman's administration complained Pataki floated Marlin's name without first consulting her. Other critics assailed Marlin's lack of experience in the public sector.
Marlin and the Port Authority were also assailed by New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who went so far as to call for abolishing the bi-state agency.

He was approved by the Port Authority board in February 1995. But not after much handwringing and open criticism of his appointment, which some felt was political pay-back to the Conservative Party for supporting Pataki's gubernatorial run.
Marlin's lack of management background also came under fire. He was a municipal porfolio manager at U.S. Trust Corp prior to taking on the Port Authority post.
More recently, his critics said Marlin has been at odds with some of Pataki's key advisers and appointees, and is being forced out of his post.
But Marlin, who stands six foot six and is the son of a New York City police officer, shrugs off the criticism.

"Governor Pataki has been very supportive of me," he said, when asked about the alledged internal strife. "When Governor Pataki originally called me, I committed to two years to changing and reprogramming the authority."
Marlin said the most difficult moments during his time in office, however, had nothing to do with his critics.

"The TWA crash was one of the great tragedies I faced here," he said, referring to the July airline crash off Long Island, which killed all 230 people aboard the airliner. "We were working around the clock with agencies and the city and state. But we proved what people are capable fo doing -- helping. It was a tragic time.
Marlin said his proudest accomplishment was "being able to make the managerial chnages here, the rightsizing of this agency."

In addition to streamlining the authority and moving back to its core mission, Marlin also noted the creation of a new monorail system for Newark Internation Airport to ferry passengers through the New Jersey airport, the start of a new international arrivals building at JFK International Airport, a proposed light rail system to JFK, and "easy pass" toll payments for the authority's tunnels and bridges.

"The projects are off the drawing table and we are getting the shovels in the ground," Marlin said. "We proved the skeptics and critics wrong. We were able to make the authority more accountable and continue to provide services to the people, while not having to raise tolls and fares."

As for Mayor Giuliani, Marlin noted the mayor had legitimate criticisms of past Port Authority practices and that they are being addresed now, including an arbitration suit over hundreds of millions of dollars in back rent the mayor says the authority owes the city.
As for some of the more strident and controversial proposals, including abolishing the bi-state agency, Marlin said, "In those areas the mayor is entitled to his opinions."
Marlin said he feels "there is a place for a regional agency to deal with issues common to New York and New Jersey."
Marlin said he had "several options out there," and politics is still one. "I am not ruling out anything at this point in time."

He is rumored to be a possible Republican candidate for New York State comptroller in 1998. During the last election, Marlin's name was bandied about, but he was not selected to run against Democratic incumbent H. Carl McCall.
